subject: Right-censorship and marginalization of joint distribution for custom likelihood

messages.author: c03edd26fd81487f
messages.subject: Right-censorship and marginalization of joint distribution for custom likelihood
parts:
Hi,

I'm trying to reproduce Random Fatigue-Limit model (Pascual & Meeker 1999, Ryan 2003 doi: 10.1198/1061860032012) using pystan. I get the model (attached .py code) to run without errors but the traces (attached picture) look like it didn't converge. 

The model describes specimen lifetime as function of stress level. There is thought to be a fatigue limit which is stochastic variable that defines whether the component will have finite lifetime or not. The joint distribution of (log(lifetime) w, fatigue limit) ~ N(b0 + b1*log(stress - fatigue_limit), sigma), and log(fatigue_limit) = v ~ N(mu_v, sigma_v). Ryan states: "When collecting fatigue data, it is possible to observe a Žfinite value of W exactly or to observe an interval that contains W. But V is not observable. Thus, for purposes of estimating \theta via methods involving a likelihood, it is necessary to obtain the marginal distribution of W. This distribution has both a continuous and a discrete component.". And because of this there is integration performed on the joint distribution to get the marginal distribution of the log(lifetime) w.

Right-censorship is needed because in practice one can't wait forever for the specimen to break. These interrupted tests, called run-outs, form the discrete component of the marginal distribution of W.

Is this model possible to be modeled in stan? My code (137 lines, including test-data) is attached. I have used the functions block to describe the puzzle pieces for the custom likelihood and numerical (trapezoidal) integration of the marginal distribution.

Thank you!
Joona

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Right-censorship and marginalization of joint distribution for custom likelihood
parts:
I don't know the specific model, but I'm familiar with
the general idea of right-censoring in these situations as
you describe and Stan should be able to fit such models.
I can make a bunch of specific suggestions about how you can
code Stan to be more robust.

The normal density and cdf are built into Stan, as is
the truncation you'd need for censored observations. So you
shouldn't be defining norm_pdf and norm_cdf. Also, you want
to work on the log scale, not on the linear scale. For
example, rather than summing a normal_pdf, you want to
log_sum_exp built-in normal_lpdf. It's much more arithmetically
stable.

That mu function can be dangerous because it's discontinuous
at the point x = v. I'm not sure why you think you need that
1e200 return, which is enormous and won't have a derivative.
We also have stable versions of log(exp(x) - exp(v)) built in


log_diff_exp(x, v) = log(exp(x) - exp(v))

and it'll be more stable than applying exp directly.

Your p_w function also has discontinuities. Stan assumes that
the log density you define is continuously differentiable.

You can't declare a parameter

real<lower=0> sigma;

and then use

log(sigma) ~ normal(0, 1);

because the log transform requires a Jacobian. Instead,
you should be using

sigma ~ lognormal(0, 1);

which builds in the Jacobian.

I also see you have some densities on non-unit scales:

b0 ~ normal(70, 35);
b1 ~ normal(-10, 5);
mu_v ~ normal(log(200), log(0.2^2 + 1));

This can make it hard for Stan to do adaptation as it has
to find the scale. One thing you can do to make this sample
better is to declare b0_raw and use

b0_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

and set

b0 = b0_raw * 35 + 70;

That puts the actual parameter being sampled, b0_raw,
on the unit scale.

You never want to do log(1 - u) for any u; use the
built in log1m(u), which is more stable. But really don't want
to take the log of p_w, you want to define p_w on the
log scale directly using log_sum_exp.

- Bob

messages.author: c03edd26fd81487f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Right-censorship and marginalization of joint distribution for custom likelihood
parts:
Hi Bob,

Thank you for your comments on this. 

I modified the code as you suggested but the traces are still not mixing well. I used the exception mu=1e200, x<v to represent a big number as the lifetime should go to infinity and I thought it'd help the numerical integration. I have now removed this exception and, instead, handle these cases in the numerical integrations. I rewrote the p_w and p_W as lp_w and lp_W respectively, as you suggested. In the log-likelihood I used log1m_exp(lp_W) for the right-censored observations.

Any further ideas why the model refuses to converge?

Regards,
Joona

parts:
Hi, I haven't looked at the detials but I'd suggest putting parameters on unit scale so you should not be having parameters such as 1e200 or even log(200) or log(75).  Put everything on unit scale and then you can use weakly informative priors such as normal(0,1) and you might get some stability.
A

messages.author: c03edd26fd81487f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Right-censorship and marginalization of joint distribution for custom likelihood
parts:
Hi,

If I understood correctly, this is what I did:
transformed parameters {
    real b0;
    real b1;
    real mu_v;
    b0 = b0_raw*35 + 75;
    b1 = b1_raw*5 - 10;
    mu_v = sqrt(log(0.2^2+1))*mu_v_raw + log(200);
    }
model {
    sigma ~ lognormal(0, 1);
    b0_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
    b1_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
    mu_v_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
    sigma_v ~ lognormal(0, 1);
    target += L(c, w, x, b0, b1, mu_v, sigma_v, sigma, N);
}

It first resulted in this kind of error:
"""
Rejecting initial value:
  Log probability evaluates to log(0), i.e. negative infinity.
  Stan can't start sampling from this initial value.



Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts. 
 Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.
"""
I added some prints to find out that my log-likelihood was giving nan's. This was fixed when I started using negative_infinity() in the numerical integration for the cases where log(0) was expected.

The code, promisingly, took longer time to run. Chain #2 was finished in 291 seconds (Total), Chain #1 took 2151 seconds, Chain #3 4182 seconds and Chain #0 4517 seconds. When I look at the traces it looks like one of the chains looks promising whereas others have remained constant value. I noticed that the chains were threaded to run on different cpus.

Any further tips on getting this to run and/or improve robustness? Would it be possible to utilize greater amount of cpus in parallel environments like computational cluster (parallelize the for-loops of the numerical integration)? Perhaps if I get this to work I should look at the ADVI for performance.

Regards,
Joona

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Right-censorship and marginalization of joint distribution for custom likelihood
parts:
We don't have any parallelization built in. You'd have to
access the C++ level and work there with a parallel interface
and be very very careful to synchronize anything that touches
autodiff.

If the sampler is getting stuck, running more chains or making
them faster won't help---the problem needs an alternative
parameterization. Getting stuck is almost always due to their
being a highly curved volume of the posterior where Stan's
adapted step size is too large.

- Bob

>> shouldn't be defining norm_pdf and norm_cdf. Also, you want
>> to work on the log scale, not on the linear scale. For
>> example, rather than summing a normal_pdf, you want to
>> log_sum_exp built-in normal_lpdf. It's much more arithmetically
>> stable.
>>
>> That mu function can be dangerous because it's discontinuous
>> at the point x = v. I'm not sure why you think you need that
>> 1e200 return, which is enormous and won't have a derivative.
>> We also have stable versions of log(exp(x) - exp(v)) built in
>>
>>
>> log_diff_exp(x, v) = log(exp(x) - exp(v))
>>
>> and it'll be more stable than applying exp directly.
>>
>> Your p_w function also has discontinuities. Stan assumes that
>> the log density you define is continuously differentiable.
>>
>> You can't declare a parameter
>>
>> real<lower=0> sigma;
>>
>> and then use
>>
>> log(sigma) ~ normal(0, 1);
>>
>> because the log transform requires a Jacobian. Instead,
>> you should be using
>>
>> sigma ~ lognormal(0, 1);
>>
>> which builds in the Jacobian.
>>
>> I also see you have some densities on non-unit scales:
>>
>> b0 ~ normal(70, 35);
>> b1 ~ normal(-10, 5);
>> mu_v ~ normal(log(200), log(0.2^2 + 1));
>>
>> This can make it hard for Stan to do adaptation as it has
>> to find the scale. One thing you can do to make this sample
>> better is to declare b0_raw and use
>>
>> b0_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
>>
>> and set
>>
>> b0 = b0_raw * 35 + 70;
>>
>> That puts the actual parameter being sampled, b0_raw,
>> on the unit scale.
>>
>> You never want to do log(1 - u) for any u; use the
>> built in log1m(u), which is more stable. But really don't want
>> to take the log of p_w, you want to define p_w on the
>> log scale directly using log_sum_exp.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>> > On Sep 15, 2016, at 2:13 AM, joona....@gmail.com wrote:
>> >
>> > Hi,
>> >
>> > I'm trying to reproduce Random Fatigue-Limit model (Pascual & Meeker 1999, Ryan 2003 doi: 10.1198/1061860032012) using pystan. I get the model (attached .py code) to run without errors but the traces (attached picture) look like it didn't converge.
>> >
>> > The model describes specimen lifetime as function of stress level. There is thought to be a fatigue limit which is stochastic variable that defines whether the component will have finite lifetime or not. The joint distribution of (log(lifetime) w, fatigue limit) ~ N(b0 + b1*log(stress - fatigue_limit), sigma), and log(fatigue_limit) = v ~ N(mu_v, sigma_v). We don't have any parallelization built in.  You'd have to
access the C++ level and work there with a parallel interface
and be very very careful to synchronize anything that touches
autodiff.

If the sampler is getting stuck, running more chains or making
them faster won't help---the problem needs an alternative
parameterization.  Getting stuck is almost always due to their
being a highly curved volume of the posterior where Stan's
adapted step size is too large.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Right-censorship and marginalization of joint distribution for custom likelihood
parts:
Usually when a chain gets stuck it's because you haven't
explored enough of the posterior during warmup and wound up
with a too-high stepsize. HMC assumes the posterior is
continuously differentiable everywhere; jumps can pose
problems for the sampler being able to move.

You can try increasing adapt_delta (target acceptance
rate) and lowering stepsize (initial step size for adaptation).
Both can help with mixing, but if the problem is pathological,
you either need to rethink the model or reparameterize.

- Bob
